scenes.visual: Dark navy canvas. Two parallel horizontal cell membranes fade in and drift gently: a presenting cell above and a T cell below. Bold white title centered: 'Two Phosphates on Partner Tails'. Schematic layout.

scenes.tts: The T cell receptor spots an infected cell. Yet its inner tail is tiny and holds no enzyme. Not even a kinase, an enzyme that adds phosphate groups. How does it fire the T cell without firing by accident?
scenes.caption: The T cell receptor spots an infected cell. Yet its inner tail is tiny and holds no enzyme. Not even a kinase, an enzyme that adds phosphate groups. How does it fire the T cell without firing by accident?
scenes.visual: Title fades out. On the top slate membrane, a slate MHC block holds a warm-white peptide. Rising from the bottom T-cell membrane, a steel-blue alpha-beta TCR grips the peptide. Zoom toward its short, stubby cytoplasmic tail; a clean red X flashes briefly over an empty enzyme slot, then fades as a glowing question mark pulses. Schematic.
scenes.narration: The T cell receptor spots an infected cell. Yet its inner tail is tiny and holds no enzyme. Not even a kinase, an enzyme that adds phosphate groups. How does it fire the T cell without firing by accident?

scenes.tts: The cell splits the job in two. The alpha and beta chains recognise a short peptide held in an M H C groove. Beside them sit partner chains called C D three and zeta. Their long inner tails carry paired tyrosines at a fixed spacing, called eye tams.
scenes.caption: The cell splits the job in two. The alpha and beta chains recognise a short peptide held in an MHC groove. Beside them sit partner chains called CD3 and zeta. Their long inner tails carry paired tyrosines at a fixed spacing, called ITAMs.
scenes.visual: Camera pulls back slightly on the same synapse. Teal CD3 and zeta partner chains slide in alongside the steel-blue alpha-beta TCR, extending long tails downward into the cytosol. On each tail, pairs of hollow gold rings appear at fixed spacing, labelled 'ITAM' (compact badge: '10 ITAMs per complex, schematic'). Rings shimmer gently.
scenes.narration: The cell splits the job in two. The alpha and beta chains recognise a short peptide held in an MHC groove. Beside them sit partner chains called CD3 and zeta. Their long inner tails carry paired tyrosines at a fixed spacing, called ITAMs.

scenes.tts: So where is the kinase? The tyrosine kinase L C K is already anchored in the T cell membrane. A share of it rides on a co-receptor, C D four or C D eight. That co-receptor grips the same M H C protein. L C K is partly active even at rest.
scenes.visual: Same synapse. An olive co-receptor (CD4/CD8) slides beside the steel-blue TCR to grip the slate MHC, carrying an amber Lck block on its inner tail; a second free amber Lck drifts along the inner membrane, glowing faintly to show it is already partly active. The teal partner tails below still carry only hollow gold rings. Schematic.
scenes.caption: So where is the kinase? The tyrosine kinase Lck is already anchored in the T cell membrane. A share of it rides on a co-receptor, CD4 or CD8. That co-receptor grips the same MHC protein. Lck is partly active even at rest.
scenes.narration: So where is the kinase? The tyrosine kinase Lck is already anchored in the T cell membrane. A share of it rides on a co-receptor, CD4 or CD8. That co-receptor grips the same MHC protein. Lck is partly active even at rest.

scenes.tts: So active L C K sits right beside those paired tyrosines in a resting cell. Yet a resting T cell stays quiet, and its tails carry no lasting phosphate. What holds the switch off?
scenes.visual: Amber Lck flashes a gold phosphate onto an ITAM ring, but the ring blinks back to hollow a moment later, again and again. Tall cool-grey stalks patrol the gap between the membranes, unlabelled for now. Question banner at top: 'Active Lck is right there. Why is a resting T cell quiet?'
scenes.caption: So active Lck sits right beside those paired tyrosines in a resting cell. Yet a resting T cell stays quiet, and its tails carry no lasting phosphate. What holds the switch off?
scenes.narration: So active Lck sits right beside those paired tyrosines in a resting cell. Yet a resting T cell stays quiet, and its tails carry no lasting phosphate. What holds the switch off?

scenes.visual: Hold on the hollow ITAM rings with the question banner 'Active Lck is right there. Why is a resting T cell quiet?' clearly readable at top. The tall grey stalks sway gently while a quiet 4.5-second progress bar glides smoothly across the bottom.

scenes.tts: A phosphatase called C D forty five keeps erasing them, because a phosphatase strips phosphate groups off. Its outer part is tall. So when the two cells press close, it no longer fits in the narrow gap. In one leading model that is what lets phosphates stay.
scenes.visual: The tall cool-grey stalks gain the label 'CD45 phosphatase' and are shown wiping a gold ring back to hollow. Then the two membranes press closer around the engaged TCR-MHC pair; the grey stalks cannot fit and slide outward to the edges (label: 'one leading model - still debated'). Inside the narrowed zone, amber Lck stays beside the teal partner tails and the gold rings now hold.
scenes.caption: A phosphatase called CD45 keeps erasing them, because a phosphatase strips phosphate groups off. Its outer part is tall. So when the two cells press close, it no longer fits in the narrow gap. In one leading model that is what lets phosphates stay.
scenes.narration: A phosphatase called CD45 keeps erasing them, because a phosphatase strips phosphate groups off. Its outer part is tall. So when the two cells press close, it no longer fits in the narrow gap. In one leading model that is what lets phosphates stay.

scenes.tts: Now watch what reads those marks. Zap seventy is a second kinase with two S H two claws, spaced to fit one pair. One phosphate holds a single claw weakly, so zap seventy slips off. That keeps a stray mark from firing the cell. With both tyrosines tagged, both claws clamp tight. Docking opens zap seventy, and L C K switches it on.
scenes.visual: Zoom on one teal partner tail. Amber Lck taps only the left ring solid gold; coral ZAP-70 with two curved SH2 claws touches it with one claw, wobbles and drifts off. Then Lck tags the second ring so BOTH rings glow bright gold, and coral ZAP-70 snaps firmly onto both at once; its folded body hinges open and Lck flashes a gold activation mark onto it.
scenes.caption: Now watch what reads those marks. ZAP-70 is a second kinase with two SH2 claws, spaced to fit one pair. One phosphate holds a single claw weakly, so ZAP-70 slips off. That keeps a stray mark from firing the cell. With both tyrosines tagged, both claws clamp tight. Docking opens ZAP-70, and Lck switches it on.
scenes.narration: Now watch what reads those marks. ZAP-70 is a second kinase with two SH2 claws, spaced to fit one pair. One phosphate holds a single claw weakly, so ZAP-70 slips off. That keeps a stray mark from firing the cell. With both tyrosines tagged, both claws clamp tight. Docking opens ZAP-70, and Lck switches it on.

scenes.tts: Here is the first core rule. Two phosphates on partner eye tams switch on the antigen receptor. Once active, zap seventy phosphorylates L A T, a membrane scaffold. Its fresh phosphotyrosines become docking bays that split the signal three ways.
scenes.caption: Here is the first core rule. Two phosphates on partner ITAMs switch on the antigen receptor. Once active, ZAP-70 phosphorylates LAT, a membrane scaffold. Its fresh phosphotyrosines become docking bays that split the signal three ways.
scenes.visual: Camera pans slightly right along the T-cell membrane while keeping the active TCR-ZAP-70 complex visible on the left. Bright coral ZAP-70 fires sparks onto a violet transmembrane bar labelled 'LAT', lighting up multiple hollow slots into bright gold docking bays.
scenes.narration: Here is the first core rule. Two phosphates on partner ITAMs switch on the antigen receptor. Once active, ZAP-70 phosphorylates LAT, a membrane scaffold. Its fresh phosphotyrosines become docking bays that split the signal three ways.

scenes.tts: Within seconds, three branches fan out from L A T. One raises calcium to send N F A T into the nucleus. A second runs through D A G and protein kinase C to N F kappa B. A third loads Ras to drive E R K and build A P one.
scenes.caption: Within seconds, three branches fan out from LAT. One raises calcium to send NFAT into the nucleus. A second runs through DAG and protein kinase C to NF-κB. A third loads Ras to drive ERK and build AP-1.
scenes.visual: Three glowing animated tracks stream downward from the gold bays on violet LAT (compact timer badge: '4–7 s, schematic'): a cyan track ('Ca²⁺ → NFAT'), an orange track ('DAG / PKC → NF-κB'), and a lime track ('Ras / ERK → AP-1'). Each pulse travels smoothly down into a dark-blue nuclear arc at the bottom.
scenes.narration: Within seconds, three branches fan out from LAT. One raises calcium to send NFAT into the nucleus. A second runs through DAG and protein kinase C to NF-κB. A third loads Ras to drive ERK and build AP-1.

scenes.tts: All three gene-switching proteins meet on target genes such as interleukin two, driving the T cell to divide. The receptor never needed its own enzyme. Partner tails carry the switch, and demanding two phosphates keeps noise from pulling the trigger.
scenes.caption: All three gene-switching proteins meet on target genes such as interleukin two, driving the T cell to divide. The receptor never needed its own enzyme. Partner tails carry the switch, and demanding two phosphates keeps noise from pulling the trigger.
scenes.visual: Inside the nuclear arc, cyan NFAT, orange NF-κB, and lime AP-1 dock side by side on a glowing DNA bar labelled 'IL-2 gene', sending a wave of light upward. Camera zooms smoothly back out to frame the whole active synapse: blue TCR on peptide-MHC, teal partner tails with paired gold phosphates, coral ZAP-70, and violet LAT.
scenes.narration: All three gene-switching proteins meet on target genes such as interleukin two, driving the T cell to divide. The receptor never needed its own enzyme. Partner tails carry the switch, and demanding two phosphates keeps noise from pulling the trigger.

scenes.visual: Synapse softens into dark navy. One clean centered line fades in at large high-contrast white type: 'Two phosphates on partner ITAMs switch on the antigen receptor.'
